what_it_does: Running a large language model (an AI that generates text) on many users' requests at the same time requires the chip to constantly read and write a large 'running notes' store — a cache of past-step results called the KV cache (short for key-value cache) — from off-chip memory chips. When the context (the amount of text the model must remember) is long, this memory traffic becomes so heavy that the arithmetic units inside the chip sit idle most of the time, wasting capacity. KVO-LLM attacks this from two sides at once: on the software side it first identifies the most important stored notes and represents them with fewer bits (a process called quantization, using smaller rounded numbers), then prunes away the least useful stored channels and time-steps guided by where the model pays attention; on the hardware side it proposes a multi-core accelerator chip that fuses several operations together and interleaves work across different users' requests to keep the math units busy and the memory bandwidth fully used. The claimed novelty is the tight coupling of algorithm-level compression with a hardware design tuned to the resulting access patterns, avoiding the accuracy loss that compression-only approaches suffer.
